#| label: ldn-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ldn_att = pd.read_csv("examples/london/data/attractions.csv")
ldn_top = ldn_att.loc[ldn_att["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
ldn_top_name = ldn_top["attraction"]
ldn_top_visits = f"{ldn_top['visits_2025']:,}"
ldn_total = f"{ldn_att['visits_2025'].sum():,}"

ldn_ch = pd.read_csv("examples/london/data/churches.csv")
ldn_ch_n = len(ldn_ch)

::: {.notes}

PDF, a dashboard, a partner brief, a flyer, a social ad and a published website
(⭐ PowerPoint, slides and an e-book). Completion: the published dashboard
URL opens on a phone. Each hands-on block ends with a checkpoint in
`quarto-workshop/checkpoints/` (01, 02 and 04); the finished project is
`quarto-workshop/examples/london/`.

new time-stamped `../london-guide-backup-NN-<time>` (earlier backups are kept), copy the
checkpoint into `london-guide/`, render, check a named file, and name the slide to rejoin
at. A checkpoint is the state at the end of its block, so it can include steps later in
that block: after catching up, skip the block's remaining prompts and follow the slides
until the next ⏱️ block starts. The room routine: anyone stuck for two minutes catches up,

## 📜 AGENTS.md: rules the assistant reads {#agents-md}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🎯]{.big}

**Scope**

what the project is, and is not
:::
::: {}
[📏]{.big}

**Rules**

what must always hold
:::
::: {}
[⌨️]{.big}

**Commands**

how to build and check it
:::
::: {}
[🔁]{.big}

**Every session**

Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity read it first
:::
:::

::: {.bigline}
✍️ say it once → every session follows it
:::

::: {.notes}
`AGENTS.md` is a plain Markdown file in the project folder. Coding assistants read it at
the start of every session, so rules written there survive a restart, a new day and a
catch-up. Codex "reads `AGENTS.md` files before doing any work"
(https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md); Antigravity reads
`AGENTS.md` or `GEMINI.md` in the project's folders (https://antigravity.google/docs/rules).
Claude Code (v2.1.277 or later) reads `AGENTS.md` when no `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`
or `CLAUDE.local.md` is in the folder or above it, and prints "AGENTS.md loaded"; if it
does not, ask it to create a `CLAUDE.md` containing `@AGENTS.md`
(https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory). All checked 2026-10-30. It is context, not enforcement: the assistant can still slip, so check
the results. Keep it short and checkable; it grows with the project, and the environment
step adds its commands. This workshop's own repository has one too.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.source .behind}
😰 Stuck?

```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/01-london-markdown/README.md
```
:::

::: {.done}
the photo shows with its credit and the link opens TfL.
:::

::: {.notes}
`[text](url)` is a link; `![caption](file)` an image. The `{...}` after the image is a
Pandoc/Quarto extension: `width` sizes it and `fig-alt` is the alt text screen readers
announce (without it the HTML image has no alt). `>` starts a blockquote. The file has
the full alt text: "Big Ben's clock tower and the Palace of Westminster against a blue sky
with white clouds." The assistant copies the photo folder; by hand it is
`cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/images .`.
Photo: "Big Ben in the sun", John Dillenbeck, CC0 1.0, file page
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Big_Ben_in_the_sun.jpg (licence and absence of
people checked 2026-10-30). The tip: 8 of London's 10 most visited ALVA attractions have free
general admission (`examples/london/data/attractions.csv`). Free tickets: the British Museum
advises booking a free ticket because entry without one depends on capacity, with queues
expected at busier times (https://www.britishmuseum.org/visit); the Natural History Museum says ticket
holders skip the queues and a free entry ticket guarantees entry
(https://www.nhm.ac.uk/visit.html). Both checked 2026-10-30.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 1 min

::: {.source .behind}

::: {.notes}
Pipes `|` separate columns; the `|---|` row marks the header, and its dash counts set the
relative column widths. An image or a link works inside a cell. The light card shows two of
the five rows, one free and one paid, so the text stays readable; the rendered `london.html`
has all five. PowerPoint tables cannot
hold pictures, so the pptx version shows each photo's alt text instead. Photos (credits in
`images/ATTRIBUTION.md`, checked 2026-10-30): British Museum, Mike Peel; Tate Modern and
National Gallery, Diego Delso; Tower of London, Dietmar Rabich (all CC BY-SA 4.0); Natural
History Museum, Julian Herzog (CC BY 4.0); all via Wikimedia Commons, with no people.
"Read more" links are each sight's official visitor page. Check what the assistant
writes: these are facts. Stations from the official visitor pages (checked 2026-10-30):
British Museum, Tottenham Court Road (britishmuseum.org/visit); Natural History Museum,
South Kensington (nhm.ac.uk/visit/getting-here.html); Tate Modern, Southwark
(tate.org.uk/visit/tate-modern); Tower of London, Tower Hill
(hrp.org.uk/tower-of-london/visit/getting-here). The National Gallery's pages name no
nearest Underground station, so that one comes from TfL: a StopPoint search around the
Gallery's coordinates (taken from the Gallery's own TfL map link) lists Charing Cross
Underground first, then Leicester Square and Embankment
(https://api.tfl.gov.uk/StopPoint/?lat=51.50893020629883&lon=-0.12829899787902832&stopTypes=NaptanMetroStation&radius=800);
station page, Bakerloo and Northern lines, Trafalgar Square:
https://tfl.gov.uk/tube/stop/940GZZLUCHX/charing-cross-underground-station. For step-free
access the Gallery suggests Tottenham Court Road or Westminster
(https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/visiting/access).
"Free" means free general admission (ALVA code 4: special exhibitions charged); the
Tower of London is "Paid" (ALVA code 1, all pay).
:::

## 🧰 Environments: then and now {#environments}

::: {.cards style="grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);"}
::: {}
[💻]{.big}

**OS**

macOS · Windows · Linux
:::
::: {}
[🔩]{.big}

**Chip**

Intel/AMD `x86_64` · Apple/ARM `arm64`
:::
::: {}
[🗣️]{.big}

**Language**

Python · R · JS … which version?
:::
::: {}
[📦]{.big}

**Dependencies**

packages · versions · compiled C
:::
:::

::: {.cards .fragment style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; margin-top: calc(0.5em * var(--ws-space));"}
::: {style="border-top-color: var(--ws-muted);"}
[🕰️]{.big}

**Then**

conda · compilers · `PATH` · kernels → ⏳ hours
:::
::: {style="border-top-color: var(--ws-green);"}
[⚡]{.big}

**Now** 🐍 `uv`

🔒 one lockfile, every OS and chip → ⏱️ seconds
:::
:::

::: {.bigline .fragment}
🤖 either way: the assistant sets it up · you approve
:::

::: {.notes}
Code runs on an operating system and a chip, in some version of its language, with
packages at particular versions. That holds for most languages, not just Python. Many
scientific packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each OS and
chip: Python ships them as wheels whose platform tag names both, such as
`macosx_11_0_arm64` ("compatibility with macOS 11 or later") or `manylinux_…_x86_64`
(https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/platform-compatibility-tags/).
Setting this up used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes
a compiler, fix `PATH`, register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on each laptop. For
Python, uv now does it in one step. It fetches Python too ("uv automatically installs
missing Python versions as needed", https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/install-python/), and
`uv.lock` "captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers
such as operating system, architecture, and Python version"
(https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/layout/), so one lockfile serves every Mac,
Windows and Linux laptop in the room. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile
the same way: R's `renv.lock` (https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html), npm's
`package-lock.json` (https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-lock-json) and
Rust's `Cargo.lock` (https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html);
all checked 2026-10-31. Either way, nobody needs to remember the commands: say what the
project needs, and the assistant runs them while you approve. The next slide does exactly
that. About a minute, no exercise, inside the block's slack.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.source .behind}
😰 Stuck?

```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/01-london-markdown/README.md
```
:::

::: {.done}
`uv run quarto check jupyter` reports the Python in this folder's `.venv`.
:::

::: {.notes}
The next section runs Python, so the guide gets its own environment first, recorded in the
folder: `pyproject.toml` lists the packages, `uv.lock` pins their exact versions, and
`.venv/` holds them. Keep the preview running: `london.md` needs no Python. Quarto needs `ipykernel`, `nbclient`, `nbformat` and `pyyaml` to run
`{python}` cells; the guide adds `pandas`, `matplotlib` and `plotly`. The bigger `jupyter`
package (JupyterLab and Notebook) is not needed. uv installs in seconds: on 2026-10-30 a
cold install of the Part 2 set took 8 s with uv and 31 s with pip plus `jupyter`, on one fast
connection. Quarto
refuses to run Python next to an unactivated `.venv` ("There is an unactivated Python
environment in .venv"), so every Quarto and Python command from here on starts with
`uv run`, which also brings `.venv` up to date from `uv.lock` first; the rule goes into
`AGENTS.md` so the assistant keeps it after a restart. A copied checkpoint
therefore rebuilds its environment on its first `uv run`. Docs, checked 2026-10-30:
https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/run/ and
https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html.
:::

## 🛟 Stuck? Catch up, then rejoin {#catch-up-drill}

::: {.bigline}
⏱️ stuck 2 min → 🛟 **Catch me up** → ➡️ next ⏱️ block
:::

both would write `london.html`. Two-space indentation matters in YAML. The preview from

now: the code and figure come next, then more formats at the end of the block, so each

::: {.prompt}

Copy ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/data here. In london.qmd, add a Python cell that reads data/attractions.csv and finds the most visited attraction and total visits_2025, plus a sentence showing both with inline code. Render it.

:::: {.columns .fragment}

````{.markdown}
```{{python}}
import pandas as pd
attractions = pd.read_csv("data/attractions.csv")

top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"

```
Most visited in 2025: the `{{python}} top_name`, with `{{python}} top_visits` visits.
London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{{python}} total_visits` visits.
````

::: {.notes}
A fence with `{python}` runs when you render, and its output lands in the document. Inline
code `` `{{python}} name` `` puts a value in a sentence, so the text never goes stale. The
syntax arrived in Quarto 1.4 (https://quarto.org/docs/blog/posts/2024-01-24-1.4-release/,
"Inline Code Syntax"). Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/computations/inline-code.html (both
checked 2026-10-30). The data folder can also be copied by hand:
`cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/data .`. The numbers on the light card are
computed by this deck from `examples/london/data/attractions.csv`: ALVA "Visits made in
2025", London rows, top ten (https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423, retrieved
2026-10-30). Only ALVA members are counted, so this is not every London sight. The 💬
question checks the idea, not the output: every inline value (the top attraction's name,
its visits and the total) updates, and nothing typed by hand does; they change at the next
render, not when the CSV is saved.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every output reads the same `data/` files and the same photo, so one update to the data
changes every audience's version at the next render. Each card names the format setting
that makes the difference, and the prompt two slides on asks for exactly these:
`format: dashboard` turns `##` headings into rows and each cell output into a card, with a
level-1 heading per page (https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/); `format: docx` is Word;
the flyer is a Typst PDF on A5 paper (`papersize: a5`,
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html#page-layout); Typst has no square paper
size, so the ad sets its page in a raw `{=typst}` block; and `project: website` in
`_quarto.yml` comes in the publishing block (docs checked 2026-10-31). The files are
`london-dashboard.qmd`, `london-email.qmd` (with `london-email-message.md`),
`london-flyer.qmd` and `london-social.qmd`. The first four are independent, so one prompt
can hand them to four sub-agents at once (next slide). The website comes last and links
them all.
:::

## 🤖 Sub-agents: one lead, many hands {#sub-agents}

::: {.cards style="grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);"}
::: {}
[🧑‍✈️]{.big}

**Lead**

your assistant: splits the work, waits, renders, checks
:::
::: {}
[🤖🤖🤖🤖]{.big}

**Sub-agents**

one task each, own context, all at once
:::
::: {}
[📄]{.big}

**One file each**

no two agents edit or render the same file
:::
:::

::: {.bigline}
⏱️ four tasks ≈ the slowest one · 🪙 more tokens
:::

[[Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) ·
[Codex](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents) ·
[Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/docs/subagents?tab=cli) · checked 2026-10-31]{.source}

::: {.notes}
A sub-agent is a separate assistant session that the lead starts for one task: it has its
own context window, does the task and reports back, while the lead waits for all of them
and checks the results. Independent tasks then take about as long as the slowest one, but
each sub-agent does its own model and tool work, so a run uses more tokens. Claude Code
runs sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them, without any set-up; its own
example is "Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using
separate subagents" (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). Codex enables sub-agents
by default and starts them when asked; its docs warn that parallel edits "can create
conflicts" and that sub-agent runs use more tokens
(https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents). Antigravity's CLI lets its
primary agent delegate to parallel subagents (https://antigravity.google/docs/subagents?tab=cli);
the docs do not say a prompt can require it, so `agy` may do the tasks itself. All checked
2026-10-31. Two rules keep parallel work safe, and the prompt states both: each sub-agent
writes only its own files and renders nothing, and the lead renders the files one at a
time, because two Quarto renders, or two `uv run` environment updates, in one folder can
collide. Sub-agents
read `AGENTS.md` too, so the project's rules (cited numbers, open photos, `uv run`) still
apply. This is the same split as this repository's own role contracts in its `AGENTS.md`.
:::

## 🗂️ One prompt, four audiences {#audiences-do}

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Run four sub-agents in parallel, one per item (none? do the items in turn). Each reads data/ and images/, hides code, follows AGENTS.md and only writes its own files: no rendering.
1. london-dashboard.qmd (format: dashboard): Attractions page (value boxes: top attraction, total `visits_2025`, number free; Plotly bars by attraction; a Plotly line of visits by `year` from data/visits.csv); Churches page (data/churches.csv, names linked to `visit_london`).
2. london-email.qmd: docx partner brief (2025 numbers as inline code, five sights with official links, getting around, sources); london-email-message.md: its covering email in a text block, no numbers.
3. london-flyer.qmd: one A5 Typst page (papersize: a5): Big Ben photo, five sights with price band and nearest tube, local tip.
4. london-social.qmd: one 12 cm square Typst page (raw Typst page size): "Visit London", photo, top attraction and its 2025 visits.
Then render the four .qmd files yourself, one at a time, and check each.
```
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 6 min

::: {.source .behind}
😰 Stuck?

```default

```
:::

::: {.done}
you open a two-page dashboard, a Word brief and its email, a one-page flyer and a square ad.
:::

::: {.notes}
One prompt, four independent jobs. Participants approve the assistant's commands and open
the four outputs; the lead starts the sub-agents, waits, then renders
`london-dashboard.qmd`, `london-email.qmd`, `london-flyer.qmd` and `london-social.qmd` in
turn and checks them; `london-email-message.md` needs no render. Ask the room to watch the
assistant report each sub-agent's progress. Finished files: `quarto-workshop/examples/london/`.

Dashboard: `format: dashboard` turns `##` headings into rows and each cell output into a
card, and a level-1 heading starts a page: "To introduce multiple pages, use level 1
headings above the level 2 headings used to define rows and columns"
(https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/data-display.html and
https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/layout.html#pages, checked 2026-10-31). `data/visits.csv`
holds 2015–2025 visits for five attractions from the ALVA yearly pages: 2020–2021 are
pandemic years, and from 2024 the Natural History Museum count includes its reopened
gardens (ALVA 2024 note v). `data/churches.csv` lists the `{python} ldn_ch_n` cathedrals and
churches on Visit London's "Cathedrals and churches in London" page
(https://www.visitlondon.com/things-to-do/sightseeing/london-attraction/historic/cathedrals-and-churches-in-london,
retrieved 2026-10-31), in page order with the page's headings as `type`: Visit London's
choice of places tourists like, not a ranking, so the page shows no visitor numbers;
`visit_london` is the church's own Visit London page, or the list itself where the list
links none. If a Plotly legend looks clipped, ask for a horizontal legend with a fixed
`entrywidth`.

Partners: Markdown headings become Word heading styles (Title, Heading 2), so the brief has
a navigable outline and its links stay clickable; `execute: echo: false` hides every code
cell. Official visitor pages: britishmuseum.org/visit, nhm.ac.uk/visit.html,
tate.org.uk/visit/tate-modern, nationalgallery.org.uk/visiting,
hrp.org.uk/tower-of-london/visit (checked 2026-10-30). The covering email is a plain `.md`
file: the `text` fence marks exactly what to copy and keeps its line breaks; to send it,
copy the `Subject:` line into the subject field and the rest into the message, and attach
`london-email.docx`. It quotes no visit numbers, so they stay in the brief, computed and
cited, as the project's rules require.

Flyer and ad: `papersize` takes any Typst paper name (`a5`, `a4`, `us-letter`, …) and
`margin` takes `x`, `y` or single sides
(https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html#page-layout, checked 2026-10-30); if the
flyer spills onto a second page, ask for a smaller photo. No paper name is square, so the ad
sets its page in a raw `{=typst}` block (`#set page(width: 12cm, height: 12cm)`; tested with
Quarto 1.6.40 and its bundled Typst 0.11) and has no title or level-1 heading, which would
land on a letter-size first page before the square one. Checkpoint 04 is the end of this
block.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
File Explorer shows your `london-guide` files and `wsl -l -v` lists Ubuntu.
:::

::: {.notes}
Windows only; on a Mac, `open .` opens the folder in Finder. Show it while the sub-agents
work: nothing here changes the project. Optional and self-paced: not counted in the agenda. Ctrl+Shift+D duplicates the Ubuntu tab in the same
folder (setup slide); the ⌄ menu beside the tabs opens a PowerShell tab. `explorer.exe .`
opens the current Linux folder in File Explorer, where double-clicking an output such as
`london-flyer.pdf` opens it in Windows. Windows drives appear under `/mnt/`, so
`/mnt/c/Users/<user>/Downloads` is your Downloads folder; keep projects in `~`, which is
faster (https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/filesystems). `code .` opens the folder in
VS Code on Windows, connected to Ubuntu, if VS Code (Windows installer, "Add to PATH") and
its WSL extension are installed (https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/tutorials/wsl-vscode);
the workshop does not need it. In PowerShell (https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/basic-commands):
`wsl -l -v` lists each distribution with its state and WSL version (from Ubuntu, type
`wsl.exe -l -v`); `wsl --user root` opens a root shell, the documented way to reset a
forgotten Linux password with `passwd <username>`
(https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/setup/environment); `wsl --shutdown` "Immediately
terminates all running distributions", so it stops the assistant and the preview: use it
only after the work is saved, for example after editing `.wslconfig`. All checked
2026-10-31. Remind the room to look back at the assistant's tab for approvals.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
Ctrl+R found your `ls` command and Ctrl+U cleared it.
:::

::: {.notes}
For everyone; also shown while the sub-agents work, optional and not counted in the agenda.
In Windows Terminal, Ctrl+Shift+C and
Ctrl+Shift+V always copy and paste. Ctrl+C copies only when text is selected; with nothing
selected it goes to the program in that tab and stops it, so in the assistant's tab it
interrupts the assistant. With the default settings a right-click copies the selection or,
with none, pastes (https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/terminal/customize-settings/actions
and https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/terminal/customize-settings/interaction). On a Mac,
Terminal uses ⌘C, ⌘V and ⌘T
(https://support.apple.com/guide/terminal/keyboard-shortcuts-trmlshtcts/mac), and Ctrl+C
still stops a command. The editing keys are defaults in Bash (Ubuntu) and zsh (macOS):
Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E jump to the start and end of the line, Ctrl+K deletes to the end, Ctrl+U
deletes to the start in Bash and the whole line in zsh, Ctrl+L clears the screen, and Ctrl+R
searches earlier commands as you type (Ctrl+R again for older matches, Enter runs it, Ctrl+G
gives up). Tab completes file and command names and lists the choices when several match.
Sources: https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bindable-Readline-Commands.html
and https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Zsh-Line-Editor.html. All checked 2026-10-31.
The exercise uses `~/quarto-workshop`, which everyone cloned, so Tab has one match.
:::

## 🌳 Git: every change, safely {#git-cycle}

::: {.bigline}
🕰️ every saved version kept · 🐙 shared on GitHub
:::

::: {.cards style="grid-template-columns: repeat(6, 1fr);"}
::: {.fragment}
[🌿]{.big}

**[branch]{translate="no"}**

`main` stays untouched
:::
::: {.fragment}
[💾]{.big}

**[commit]{translate="no"}**

a snapshot + why
:::
::: {.fragment}
[☁️]{.big}

**[push]{translate="no"}**

copy it to GitHub
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔀]{.big}

**[pull request]{translate="no"}**

propose the change
:::
::: {.fragment}
[👀]{.big}

**[review]{translate="no"}**

someone reads the diff
:::
::: {.fragment}
[✅]{.big}

**[merge]{translate="no"}**

into `main`
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .bigline}
👤 today: straight to `main` · 👥 a team: the whole loop
:::

::: {.notes}
Concepts, not commands: the assistant runs git and you approve. The six terms stay in
English when the deck is translated, as they do in git and on GitHub. A repository is the
project folder plus its full history. A commit is a snapshot of every tracked file with a
message saying why, so any earlier version can be restored or compared. A branch is a
movable label on a line of commits: work happens on a branch while `main` stays working
(https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Branches-in-a-Nutshell). Push copies commits
to the remote repository on GitHub. A pull request proposes merging a branch, shows the
diff and collects discussion and checks
(https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests);
a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes
(https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/reviewing-changes-in-pull-requests/about-pull-request-reviews);
merging adds its commits to `main`. All checked 2026-10-31. Working alone today, the next
slides commit straight to `main` and push; in a team, every change goes round the loop,
and this workshop's own repository is built that way. Ask the assistant to "commit with a
message that says why", and read its diffs before you approve.
:::

## 🌐 GitHub Pages {#gh-pages}

![](assets/gh-pages-flow.svg){fig-alt="Three steps: your source lives in a GitHub repository; quarto publish gh-pages renders the site and pushes the HTML to a gh-pages branch; GitHub serves that branch at user.github.io/repo." width="92%"}

::: {.bigline}
🆓 free static hosting, straight from a GitHub repo
:::

::: {.notes}
GitHub Pages serves static files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PDFs) from a repository branch.
Quarto renders locally and pushes only the rendered site to a `gh-pages` branch.
:::

## 🏗️ A project: one folder → one website {#london-website}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (render only the .qmd files; navbar: Guide, Dashboard, a Downloads menu for the docx, pdf, pptx, epub and london-slides.html files that exist), index.qmd, and a .gitignore for /_site/, /.quarto/ and /.venv/. Render and check the links.
```
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.ldn-src}
```{.yaml}
project:
  type: website
website:
  title: "Visit London"
  navbar:
    left:
      - {text: Guide, href: london.qmd}
      - {text: Dashboard, href: london-dashboard.qmd}
      - {text: Downloads, menu: [...]}
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.agent}
writes 3 files · `uv run quarto render` → `_site/`
:::

::: {.you}
`uv run quarto preview`
:::
:::
::::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 3 min

::: {.source .behind}
😰 Stuck?

```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/README.md
```
:::

::: {.done}
the site opens with Guide, Dashboard and Downloads.
:::

::: {.notes}
A `_quarto.yml` makes the folder a project: `quarto render` builds every listed page into
`_site/`, with shared navigation, and the dashboard becomes a page of the site. The full
file is `quarto-workshop/examples/london/_quarto.yml`: its `render` list keeps README and
attribution notes from becoming pages, and the Downloads menu links `london.docx`,
`london.pdf`, `london.pptx`, `london.epub`, `london-slides.html`, `london-email.docx`, `london-flyer.pdf` and
`london-social.pdf`; a participant's menu lists only the files they made, as the ⭐ ones
may be missing. Part 1 has no checkpoint after 04: the catch-up prompt copies the
finished project, `quarto-workshop/examples/london/`.
:::

## 🚀 Publish {#london-publish}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Initialise a git repository here and commit everything except _site/, .quarto/ and .venv/. Then create a public GitHub repository named `london-guide` with gh and push to it.
```
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Publish the site with `uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt` and tell me the live URL.
```
:::

::: {.you}
approve the `gh` and `quarto publish` commands · open the URL on your phone 📱 · 404? wait a minute, reload
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 5 min

::: {.source .behind}
😰 Stuck?

```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/README.md
```
:::

::: {.done}
`https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html` opens on your phone 📱
:::

::: {.notes}
The assistant runs `gh repo create london-guide --public --source=. --push`, which creates
the GitHub repository from this folder and pushes the commits
(https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create), using the `gh` sign-in from the setup check.
`quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt` skips the confirmation question an assistant cannot
answer (`quarto publish --help`, Quarto 1.6.40); it renders locally, creates the `gh-pages`
branch on its first run, pushes the site and opens it. For a project site no
Settings → Pages change is needed; that page shows the URL and status
(https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html,
checked 2026-10-30). Alternative: a GitHub Action renders on every push using
`quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2` and `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2` with
`target: gh-pages`; run `quarto publish gh-pages` once locally first, and the Action needs
Python and the packages (or `freeze: auto` with `_freeze/` committed). The finished project
is `quarto-workshop/examples/london/`; Part 1 has no checkpoint after 04.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every number in Part 1 comes from `examples/london/data/attractions.csv` or `visits.csv`
(`churches.csv` lists Visit London's churches, with no numbers);
each row carries its source URL and retrieval date. ALVA lists only its members' sites.
VisitBritain's town-level inbound visits were considered but left out. Its page
(https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/inbound-visits-and-spend-trends-uk-town,
checked 2026-10-30) warns that 2024 data are "official statistics in development", that the
ONS does not endorse 2024 comparisons with previous years, and that the page does not yet
reflect the revised 2024 estimates released on 4 September 2026.
:::
